title: Sold Zip2 to Compaq and rolled the proceeds into online banking
statement: In February 1999 Musk sold the online city-guide software company Zip2, founded with Kimbal Musk and Greg Kouri in 1995, to Compaq for $307 million in cash, collecting $22 million for his 7 percent share after the board blocked his bid to become chief executive.
outcome: Musk recycled the entire proceeds into X.com, the online financial-services and e-mail-payment company he co-founded that same year, beginning the serial-compounding pattern that produced PayPal.

title: Founded SpaceX with $100 million of his own PayPal fortune
statement: After two Moscow trips failed to secure repurposed intercontinental ballistic missiles for a Mars greenhouse project, Musk founded Space Exploration Technologies in May 2002 with roughly $100 million of his own early fortune, betting that vertical integration and software-style modality could cut launch costs.
outcome: The fourth Falcon 1 flight reached orbit in September 2008 on the company's last money, and NASA's $1.6 billion Commercial Resupply Services contract that December saved the company, making SpaceX the leading global launch provider by 2017 with a 45 percent share of awarded commercial contracts.

title: Led Tesla's Series A round and took the chairmanship
statement: In February 2004 Musk invested $6.5 million of Tesla Motors' $7.5 million Series A round, becoming the largest shareholder and chairman of the company incorporated the prior July by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning, while overseeing Roadster product design.
outcome: After the 2008 financial crisis forced out Eberhard, Musk assumed the chief-executive role in October 2008 and carried Tesla to a $1 trillion market capitalization in October 2021; a 2009 settlement designated him a Tesla co-founder.

title: Published the Tesla master plan staircase strategy
statement: Musk laid out Tesla's 2006 master plan: build a premium sports car for early adopters, use the proceeds to fund progressively more mainstream vehicles including sedans and affordable compacts, and pair the fleet with solar generation co-marketed with SolarCity.
outcome: The staircase was executed almost literally, from roughly 2,500 Roadsters to the Model S, Model X, and the mass-market Model 3, which became the world's best-selling electric car from 2018 through 2021.

title: Acquired SolarCity and folded it into Tesla Energy
statement: Tesla announced the all-stock $2.6 billion acquisition of SolarCity, the solar installer his cousins founded on his concept and capital, in 2016, merging it with Tesla's battery unit as Tesla Energy despite the target's undisclosed liquidity problems.
outcome: Shareholder litigation followed for years, with Tesla directors settling in January 2020 and the Delaware court ruling in Musk's favor in 2022 as the sole remaining defendant; more than 85 percent of unaffiliated shareholders had approved the deal.

title: Bet Tesla's solvency on the Model 3 volume ramp
statement: Tesla announced the Model 3 in April 2016 as its first mass-market vehicle at a $35,000 price point, collected more than 325,000 reservations within a week, and advanced its 500,000-unit build plan to 2018, financing the ramp with a $2 billion share issuance and heavy factory automation.
outcome: The automation initially slowed output into what the company called production hell, with just 2,425 cars built in the fourth quarter of 2017, but the 5,000-per-week target was met in mid-2018 and the Model 3 became the world's best-selling plug-in car.

title: Settled the SEC funding-secured fraud suit
statement: Two days after the SEC sued him over the August 2018 tweet claiming funding was secured for taking Tesla private, Musk settled without admitting or denying the allegations, accepting a $20 million personal fine and a three-year step-down as Tesla chairman while remaining chief executive.
outcome: Tesla paid a separate $20 million fine, a 2019 contempt dispute produced a clarified agreement requiring preclearance of market-moving topics, and a 2023 shareholder jury found Musk and Tesla not liable over the tweet.

title: Completed the $44 billion acquisition of Twitter
statement: After attempting to terminate the merger over spambot disclosures and losing early rulings in the Delaware Court of Chancery, Musk closed the $44 billion purchase of Twitter on October 27, 2022, funded with $13 billion of bank debt, $6.25 billion of personal loans against his Tesla stock, and roughly $27 billion of equity.
outcome: He cut headcount about 80 percent to roughly 1,500, rebranded the platform as X in July 2023, and in March 2025 folded it into xAI in an all-stock transaction valuing the combined enterprise at $45 billion.
